articles.title: Witchers and Battles of Spirits
articles.excerpt: Tradition about the «witchers» — sorcerers who combat malevolent spirits in Elis, Achaia, and Ilia.

content.value: "The spirit of the Ovrya seeks the alliance of a man to destroy the rival spirit. This man is not from the same village, but a witcher from another neighbouring village. The witchers are the enemies of malevolent spirits. Like the Nereid-seers and masters, the Nereid-handlers have the power to heal the wounds caused by sprites, by appeasing them, while the witcher subjugates and combats the spirits, rendering them harmless. The tradition describes how the witcher, when brought from a distant village, destroyed and routed a very dangerous smerdaki.

The witchers are light-shadowed, possessing the natural ability to see the heavy-shadowed ones — the invisible sprites — while they have also learned the art of combating them. Their large population lived in earlier times in Elis and in some villages of Achaia and Ilia, but for many years there has been no one, or at least no one known as such outside their own village."

The text refers to the mythology and traditions of villages concerning spirits and their battles. The «witchers» are described as sorcerers or specialists who can protect their villages from malevolent spirits, using abilities to appease or combat supernatural creatures. These creatures may include ghosts or other supernatural entities that cause problems for people.
Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, N. G. Politis – Traditions, Part B, 1904 – pp. 1119–1120

articles.title: The Witcher – Spirit Exorcist
articles.excerpt: Detailed description of the rituals for exorcising «zoudia» by witchers in villages of Elis and Achaia, with historical examples.

content.value: "If one or two sudden deaths occurred in a village, or a suicide or accident, these were attributed to some influence from the spirit (zoudio), and it was considered necessary to drive out the spirit for the salvation of the village. Similarly, if frequent deaths or serious illnesses were observed in a house, it was believed to be haunted. The danger to the house's inhabitants could only be neutralised if the spirit was expelled. To this end, they summoned the witcher, who never came willingly, always raising various objections, until he was finally persuaded by the villagers' earnest entreaties and their promises of generous reward. If he needed to purify a haunted house, he ordered it to be emptied, with all the furniture and utensils removed, leaving the walls bare."

"Then he entered the house with three companions who held pistols loaded with blank cartridges, and tried to discover in which corner the spirit was hiding. If he had to free the village from the zoudio, his first task was to locate it. For this he went through all the houses of the village, followed by many, carefully examining every corner and hiding place. When after much searching and effort he located the zoudio, he would wink slyly at his companions, saying 'Here is the friend!' He then gave the order to arm the village's young men with firearms, to help him drive out the spirit, loading the weapons with blank cartridges."

"And so silence had to be maintained, because 'if anyone speaks, the zoudio will take their speech'; they had to be ready to shoot with the left hand whenever he gave the signal. He then returned to the house where he had found the zoudio and began shooting at it with the index finger of his left hand, giving the signal to his followers to shoot along with him. After many bangs and shots and shouts to frighten the obstinate zoudio, he assured his followers that he had managed 'to drive it out of that house'. It was necessary to prevent the zoudio from entering another house. The village had been emptied of its inhabitants, as all had shut their homes in accordance with the witcher's orders and had gone out to the fields. He ran through the streets with his helpers, pursuing the zoudio with shouts and gunshots."

"And so the zoudio, being pursued, took refuge in dense hedges, which the witcher followed into, though the thorns and brambles tore his clothes. When he overcame its refuges, the zoudio left the village and, now exhausted, would sit on a tree or in ruins. But soon the witcher too would run and, with great effort, catch it by the legs and pin it to the spot with a large new pitchfork — sometimes four of them — one nailed into its head, another into its heart, and the other two into its legs. Having concluded the struggle, the witcher, drenched in sweat, would sing of the adventures of the battle. He would typically describe the zoudio as fearsome and enormous, saying it had tormented him greatly and he had risked being torn apart by it, had it not been for the precious help of the True Cross which he wore as an amulet."

"He then received the agreed reward and was sent off with honour by the grateful villagers, returning to his own, where he usually found similar invitations from other villages. According to Mr Koryllos, the witcher received many such invitations during the summer months, when many malignant fevers accompanied by convulsions or sudden deaths occurred — because, as people believed, the zoudio was consuming them."

"But once the use of quinine became widespread among the villagers too, the effects of combating the miasma became perceptible and were considerably reduced, with the result that the «witchers» were rendered obsolete."

"In the report of the communications of Ch. P. Koryllos, a physician in Patras, in his account of the 'witchers', there was before him a narrative written around the middle of the previous century, published anonymously in the newspaper Estia in 1896. In the issue of 10 August, the anonymous author describes how, in 1829, the witcher cleansed the haunted house in Gastouni of Elis of its 'zoudio'."

articles.title: The Spirit of Veliziou and the Witcher
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about the spirit of Veliziou and the magical practices of the witcher Giorgis Kapitanios

content.value: The spirit of Veliziou dwelt in the mulberry tree, the tree that to this day stands outside the village. It too was a star-marked ox, for it had a star on its forehead, while the spirit of the Ovrya had none. It would fight with the spirit of the Ovrya and defeat it, and great evil came about in the surrounding area.

One night a witcher, Giorgis Kapitanios from Mirali, heard a voice telling him to rise and shoot dead the star-marked ox. He rose and saw it fighting with the spirit of the Ovrya, and he shot at it with his left hand and killed the star-marked ox. And so the spirit of Veliziou vanished.

That witcher would nail down spirits, and he also nailed the spirit of Soulion, which appeared as an old man. And for this reason, one time when the witcher was going to Gourzoumiasa, the spirits gathered together, appeared as hounds, and devoured him, and he died.

And when he died, they searched him and found no bite marks from a dog anywhere, though they had heard the commotion and the evil that had taken place when they attacked him to devour him, down in the ravine.

articles.title: Pagondas Cemetery on Samos – A Witcher Exorcises Vrykolakes
articles.excerpt: Story of a witcher who exorcises vrykolakes from the Pagondas cemetery using a ritual involving three oxen.

content.value: Many years ago, many people in the Pagondas cemetery were becoming vrykolakes. So many, that the local inhabitants each gave an «aspro» coin to a witcher who performed the «enthronement» ritual — that is, he circled the entire cemetery three times with three oxen born of the same cow, while reciting certain strange words. From that time on, no one ever became a vrykolakas again in that particular cemetery.

The same witcher offered to perform the same procedure throughout the entire village to protect it from sprites — or as they are referred to in the area, «evil enchantments» — asking for 3 aspra from each inhabitant. However, the sum was large and the inhabitants could not pay it.

The incident became known throughout Samos and in nearby areas, so that people from outside the island came and took soil from that particular cemetery, carrying it to their own cemeteries to combat potential vrykolakes. Some others made the soil into an amulet and hung it on the walls of their homes as protection against vrykolakes.

articles.title: The Sabbatian at Lakovikia
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: Tradition from Mesolakkia in Serres about the Sabbatian (born on a Saturday) and his protective little dog that gives him courage against vrykolakes and renders him invisible — visible only to the dog.

image.alt: Traditional dog in the Macedonian countryside, symbol of protection against vrykolakes

content.value: In Lakovikia (now Mesolakkia) it is believed that the Sabbatian owes his power to a small dog, which follows him every night and gives him the courage not to fear the Vrykolakas.
It is also said that the Sabbatian, in these circumstances, is invisible to everyone except the small dog.

articles.title: The Destruction of the Vrykolakas by the Sabbatian
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: Macedonian folkloric narrative about a Sabbatian (born on a Saturday) who destroyed a vrykolakas in Sochos. He lured it into counting millet, then nailed it to the wall — echoing folk songs that describe similar rituals.

content.value: People who were born on a Saturday (and are therefore called «Sabbatians») are believed to possess the undoubted privilege of seeing ghosts and spectral visions, as well as having great influence over vrykolakes.

A local man from Sochos assured the author that one such person had managed to lure a vrykolakas into a stable and set him to counting the seeds from a heap of millet. While the demon was occupied with the counting, the Sabbatian attacked him and managed to nail him to the wall.

The story presents several points of interest. First, the nailing of an evil being to the wall is an idea well known in Macedonian tradition. It appears even in folk songs. Indeed, I heard a children's rhyme from a girl of the same village, which began with the words:
"Spirit buried deep
To the wall nailed fast"...
